basedOn.source: Jacob Charnock (GovAI): Third-party AI evaluation contracts should be published

criteria.name: Scope is public
criteria.standard: For each outside evaluation, the lab publishes what was checked: which risks and claims, which models, and what was left out.
parts: Scope is published for every outside evaluation
It says which risks and claims were checked
It says which models
It says what was left out
criteria.why: A clean result means little if you can't see what wasn't looked at.
criteria.model: The Evaluation covers [risks and claims] for [models]. It does not cover [exclusions]. The Company will publish this scope, including the exclusions, alongside the Evaluator's report.

criteria.name: Access is public
criteria.standard: Published terms say what evaluators can see (models and checkpoints, internal documents, staff), whether they can ask for more, and when the lab can refuse. Evaluators can say publicly when access was too limited.
parts: Published terms say what evaluators can see
They say whether evaluators can ask for more
They say when the lab can refuse
Evaluators can say publicly when access was too limited
criteria.why: Findings are only as strong as the evidence the evaluator was allowed to see.
criteria.model: The Evaluator will have access to [models, checkpoints, documents, systems and staff]. The Evaluator may request further information relevant to the Evaluation, and the Company will give written reasons for any refusal. The Evaluator may state publicly what access it had and where it considers that access insufficient.

criteria.name: Evaluators control what they publish
criteria.standard: The evaluator decides what to publish. The lab can only require redactions in categories agreed before the work starts (like trade secrets, security details or customer data), can't block or soften findings, and the evaluator can say when redactions affected its conclusions. Serious concerns can go to the lab's board or a regulator.
parts: The evaluator decides what to publish, without the lab's approval
The lab can only require redactions in categories agreed beforehand
The evaluator can say when redactions affected its conclusions
Serious concerns can go to the lab's board or a regulator
criteria.why: If the lab can edit or veto the report, the report is partly the lab's.
criteria.model: The Evaluator has final editorial control over its report. The Company may require redaction only of information in the categories listed in [Schedule X], agreed before the Evaluation began, and may not require changes to the Evaluator's findings or conclusions. The Evaluator may state where and why material was redacted, and whether redactions affected its conclusions. The Evaluator may raise serious concerns directly with the Company's board or a relevant government authority.

criteria.name: Pay doesn't depend on findings
criteria.standard: Published terms say who pays for the evaluation and how the fee is set, and that no payment depends on what the evaluator finds.
parts: Published terms say who pays
They say how the fee is set
They say no payment depends on the findings
criteria.why: An evaluator paid more for good news has a reason to find it.
criteria.model: The Company will pay the Evaluator a fixed fee of [amount], set before the Evaluation begins. No part of the fee, or any future engagement, depends on the Evaluator's findings or conclusions.

criteria.name: Conflict rules are public
criteria.standard: Published conflict-of-interest rules for evaluators: no equity in the lab, no financial dependence on it, limits on other paid work for the lab, and what must be disclosed or lead to someone stepping aside.
parts: Evaluators hold no equity in the lab
They aren't financially dependent on it
There are limits on other paid work for the lab
The rules say what must be disclosed or lead to stepping aside
criteria.why: Readers need to know whether the evaluator has reasons to go easy on the lab.
criteria.model: The Evaluator and its staff working on the Evaluation hold no equity or debt in the Company. The Evaluator will disclose in its report any other paid work for the Company in the past [two] years, and any staff member with a close personal or financial tie to the Company will step aside from the Evaluation.

criteria.name: Term and renewal are public
criteria.standard: Published length of each engagement, and how renewal or ending it is decided, including that the lab can't end or decline to renew it because of the findings.
parts: The length of each engagement is published
So is how renewal or ending is decided
The lab can't end or decline to renew it because of the findings
criteria.why: The threat of losing the next contract can shape a report as much as a veto can.
criteria.model: This agreement runs from [date] to [date]. The Company may not end this agreement, or decline to renew it, because of the Evaluator's findings. Any decision not to renew will be published with its reasons.

ratings.evidence: Anthropic has published what its main outside evaluations cover: Faculty (Accenture's AI business) on red-teaming, alignment assessments and safeguard testing; SecureBio on the chemical and biological weapons chapter of its August 2026 Risk Report; and a METR team embedded inside the company. For one evaluation the full scope is public: in Transluce's August 2026 mental health study, the published agreement says which behaviours were checked and Transluce's report lists the Claude models tested. It's "Partly" because the rest are announcements, not per-evaluation scopes, and they don't list what was left out.
ratings.source: Anthropic: An update on independent evaluators

additionalSources.source: Anthropic: Accenture embedded evaluation
Transluce: Mental Health Behavior Report

ratings.evidence: Anthropic describes three tiers of access. At the top tier, six METR staff have company hardware, office space and internal tools, close to its own risk teams, and staff are encouraged to share everything except customer data, privileged legal advice and model architecture. METR may comment on the access it had. It's "Partly" because Anthropic sets lower-tier access case by case, says there are no standards yet for what embedded evaluators should see, and hasn't published the agreements.
ratings.source: Anthropic: An update on independent evaluators

additionalSources.source: Anthropic: Accenture embedded evaluation

ratings.evidence: At its upper two tiers, Anthropic says it can't veto publication and can only require redactions in predefined categories, and evaluators can publish their view on whether redactions were justified. But first-tier findings are published only with Anthropic's approval, Anthropic decides what falls in the redaction categories, and it told Reuters it keeps the right to comment on and approve reports from newer evaluators. No route to the board or a regulator is described. In the agreement Transluce published for its August 2026 mental health study, Transluce had the final say on publishing its evaluation findings, and Anthropic could block the validation results only on listed grounds, not for poor performance. SecureBio says it can publish its review of a chapter of Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report without Anthropic's approval, that Anthropic can mark sensitive material for redaction at its discretion, and that its report will say whether redactions affected its findings. METR says its contract wording lets it disclose any publishing limits or redaction steps it's under, though not all its past work meets that bar, and that it's starting to add terms for taking findings to a lab's board.
ratings.source: Anthropic: An update on independent evaluators

ratings.evidence: Anthropic says it funds Faculty's embedded evaluation directly. It hasn't published how the fee is set or said that payment doesn't depend on findings. METR's conflict-of-interest policy says METR hasn't yet been paid for company-identifying risk assessments.

additionalSources.source: METR conflict-of-interest policy v1.1

ratings.evidence: Anthropic says evaluators shouldn't hold equity in the company or be financially or operationally dependent on it, and that METR's embedded team is walled off from METR's other Anthropic work. It hasn't published rules on other paid work for Anthropic or what evaluators must disclose, and it is paying Faculty directly.
ratings.source: Anthropic: An update on independent evaluators

ratings.evidence: The agreement Anthropic signed with Transluce for its August 2026 mental health study, which Transluce published, runs until the study is finished. Either side can end it with seven business days' notice, and Transluce's right to publish survives if it's ended. It's "Partly" because nothing stops Anthropic ending it over the findings, and no length or renewal terms are public for its safety evaluators. The "at least $1 billion over five years" Anthropic and Accenture announced is an investment plan, not a contract term.
ratings.source: Transluce: template evaluation agreement (mental health study)

ratings.evidence: OpenAI describes the kinds of outside assessment it uses (independent evaluations, methodology reviews and expert probing) and names assessors including METR, SecureBio, Apollo Research and Irregular. For its Hugging Face incident review, METR published the agreed scope and what was out of scope. In Transluce's August 2026 mental health study, the published agreement says which behaviours were checked and Transluce's report lists the OpenAI models tested. Scope isn't published for each evaluation as a rule.

ratings.evidence: OpenAI says assessors have had early checkpoints, models with fewer safeguards and, for some, direct chain-of-thought access, with public or production models as the default. METR's Hugging Face review spelled out its access: six days on site and over a thousand transcripts, but no direct access to OpenAI's systems. There are no published terms on when more access can be requested or refused.
ratings.source: OpenAI: Strengthening safety with external testing

additionalSources.source: METR: OpenAI Hugging Face incident investigation

ratings.evidence: Contract excerpts OpenAI published in Nov 2025 say assessors must get OpenAI's written approval before publishing, and OpenAI says it reviews for confidentiality and factual accuracy. In Oct 2026 OpenAI told Reuters it doesn't seek approval over full reports, redacts confidential information, and lets evaluators say when major redactions were made. For its Hugging Face review, METR said OpenAI could redact any non-public information and that it edited tone and emphasis after OpenAI's feedback. Newer contract wording for its safety assessors isn't public. In the agreement Transluce published for its August 2026 mental health study, Transluce had the final say on publishing its evaluation findings, and OpenAI could block the validation results only on listed grounds, not for poor performance. METR says its contract wording lets it disclose any publishing limits or redaction steps it's under, though not all its past work meets that bar, and that it's starting to add terms for taking findings to a lab's board. It doesn't name the labs.

It hasn't published how fees are set. METR says it took no payment for its Hugging Face review, though OpenAI provided free API credits.

ratings.evidence: Google DeepMind hasn't published the scope of any outside evaluation. For one evaluation the scope is public anyway: Transluce's August 2026 study of how AI systems respond to users in a mental health crisis. The agreement Google DeepMind signed, which Transluce published, says which behaviours the study checks, and Transluce's report lists the Gemini models it tested. It's "Partly" because that's one study, published by Transluce and not Google, and it isn't one of Google DeepMind's safety evaluations.
ratings.source: Transluce: template evaluation agreement (mental health study)

additionalSources.source: Transluce: Mental Health Behavior Report

ratings.evidence: For one evaluation, what the evaluator could see is public. For its August 2026 mental health study, Transluce says Google DeepMind gave it testing access at no cost, through a nonpublic API meant to match the Gemini app, and signed a confidentiality agreement so it could receive privileged information about its systems' behaviour and safeguards. Transluce also says deeper access, like chains of thought and model internals, would allow more. The agreement itself says only that the developer "may provide the Evaluator with privileged system access as necessary". It's "Partly" because nothing says whether Transluce could ask for more or when Google could refuse, and no access terms are public for Google DeepMind's safety evaluators.
ratings.source: Transluce: mental health report, independence and transparency disclosure

additionalSources.source: Transluce: Announcing Transluce's Mental Health Evaluation
Transluce: template evaluation agreement (mental health study)

ratings.evidence: In the one contract that's public, the evaluator has the final say. Under the agreement Google DeepMind signed with Transluce for its August 2026 mental health study, Google sees a draft 30 days before publication and can give feedback, but Transluce has "final discretion to redact or publish" the findings. Transluce's own disclosure says the same: the labs got early access to results, "but not control" over them. It's "Partly" because this is one study, and Transluce published the agreement, not Google. It doesn't say Transluce can flag redactions that affected its conclusions, and there's no route to Google's board or a regulator. Google DeepMind hasn't published terms for its safety evaluators. As of Sept 2026 it hadn't committed to embedding them; Demis Hassabis instead proposed an industry standards body to test frontier models, TechCrunch reported.
ratings.source: Transluce: template evaluation agreement (mental health study)

additionalSources.source: Transluce: mental health report, independence and transparency disclosure

Transluce also says it never takes pay that depends on its findings, but that's Transluce's own policy, not a term Google has published. It's "Partly" because that's one study, and nothing public says how Google DeepMind pays its other evaluators.
